corpus.title: US cancels joint marine drills with South Korea over Iran war-related force constraints
corpus.signal_text:
The United States canceled a joint amphibious landing drill scheduled for next month with South Korea, Seoul’s Marine Corps said on Monday, after Washington cited constraints on the availability of U.S. forces due to the war in Iran.
The U.S. Marine Corps formally notified its South Korean counterpart in June that force availability would be constrained for the division-level exercise, known as Ssangyong, a South Korean Marine Corps spokesperson told a press briefing.
The allies remain in close consultations on resuming the drills, the spokesperson said. He did not specify what measures might be taken to prevent future cancelations or to make up for lost training opportunities.
U.S. Forces Korea did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Later on Monday, the U.S. State Department said that Secretary of State Marco Rubio had spoken with South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun about a “range of issues” in their alliance.
Rubio told his South Korean counterpart that Washington and Seoul need to remain in close coordination on matters integral to their alliance, according to a State Department statement.
The cancelation of the amphibious landing drill follows U.S. President Donald Trump’s surprise order to scale back a separate annual joint military exercise that ended last Friday, citing the cost and Seoul’s refusal to take part in the Iran war.
Trump also wrote on his Truth Social platform that the Ulchi Freedom Shield drills sent “a signal that was totally inappropriate and hostile, to a Country that, as long as Donald J. Trump has been President, has been unthreatening and respectful.” Despite the reduction of the exercises, Pyongyang fired 10 short-range ballistic missiles last week and issued a statement denouncing the exercises.
North Korea has long condemned such joint exercises as rehearsals for invasion.

corpus.title: S. Korea, U.S. remain committed to N.K. denuclearization despite omission from call readouts: Seoul
corpus.signal_text:
S. Korea, U.S. remain committed to N.K. denuclearization despite omission from call readouts: Seoul
By Oh Seok-min
SEOUL, Aug. 25 (Yonhap) -- South Korea and the United States remain committed to the goal of denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula despite the omission of the term from the readouts of their top diplomats' latest phone call, Seoul's foreign ministry said Tuesday.
The ministry made the comment after its press release on Monday's call between Foreign Minister Cho Hyun and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio referred to "the resolution of the North Korean nuclear issue" but did not explicitly mention denuclearization.
 The U.S. State Department's separate readout of the talks also did not mention Pyongyang's nuclear issue or denuclearization. State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott simply said Rubio noted the need for the two countries to "remain in close coordination on matters that are integral to the alliance."
"South Korea and the U.S. have consistently maintained the goal of peace, stability and denuclearization on the Korean Peninsula, as stated in the joint explanatory material following the South Korea-U.S. summit in November last year," ministry spokesperson Park Do-sun said at a regular press briefing.
Seoul and Washington have been pursuing their North Korea policies "through close coordination to achieve the aforementioned goal, and related discussions also took place during this latest phone call between the foreign ministers," he added.
Questions have grown over whether the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump is placing less emphasis on the long-standing goal of denuclearizing North Korea as Trump seeks to reengage with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un.
Trump said he expects to meet Kim again later this year, while declining last week to say whether denuclearization remains his goal in seeking to reengage with Kim.
South Korea and the U.S. also scaled back their combined military exercises last week at Trump's direction, a move seen as a conciliatory gesture toward Pyongyang.
